background.definition: Renal cell cancer (RCC), also known as kidney cancer or renal cancer, is a disease in which malignant cells arise from the renal tubule epithelium; 90% of kidney cancers are RCC of predominantly clear cell histology. The remaining subtypes are papillary, chromophobe, collecting duct, and medullary (occurs in patients with sickle cell trait or disease). Renal masses located in the pelvis are primarily transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) and treatment is similar to that for bladder carcinoma.

list.listitem: Estimated new cases in 2020 in US from SEER registry 73,750 cases with an expected 14,830 deaths.
Globally there are an estimated 403,000 people diagnosed with kidney cancer and 175,000 deaths.
The ratio of males to females globally is approximately 2:1.
Tobacco
Obesity
Genetic factors (see pathophysiology section below)
Occupational exposure (asbestos, cadmium, petroleum products, herbicides, trichloroethylene)
Hypertension
Alcohol
End-stage renal disease
Polycystic kidney disease
RCC is caused by acquired or sporadic mutations in tumor suppressor genes (eg, von Hippel-Lindau syndrome) or proto-oncogenes (eg, c-MET, fumarate hydratase).
See for genetic syndromes associated with renal cancer.
Screening of asymptomatic individuals is not recommended because of the low prevalence of RCC in the general population. C
Perform complete history and physical, laboratory tests, and urinalysis. C
Order abdominal/pelvic CT scan or MRI scan. B
Only order bone scan or brain MRI if metastases to those sites are suspected. B
There is currently no role for PET scan. B

list.listitem: The classic triad of flank pain, hematuria, and palpable abdominal mass is only noted in 9% of patients. In addition to these symptoms, patients may present with fever, diaphoresis, weight loss, and bony or visceral pain.

A systematic review concluded that CT urography (LR+ 94, LR- 0.06) was more accurate than MR urography (LR+ 5.9, LR- 0.2) for the diagnosis of renal cell cancer in patients presenting with either microscopic or gross hematuria.
Scrotal varicoceles that do not empty or reduce upon recumbency may be observed.
Focal neurologic deficits may be caused by intracranial metastasis.
Paraneoplastic syndromes: anemia, erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia.
Among patients presenting with microscopic hematuria, a systematic review of 30 studies with 24, 366 patients found a diagnostic yield after evaluation of 0.18% for renal cell cancer.
If renal cell cancer is suspected based on symptoms, order CT of abdomen and pelvis.
Initial evaluation of the newly diagnosed patient should include CBC, comprehensive metabolic profile including lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and urinalysis.
In patients to be treated with targeted agents, obtain a test of thyroid function.
CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis is moderately sensitive and very specific for detection of renal vein invasion, metastatic adenopathy, perinephric invasion, and adjacent organ invasion.

PET scan: accuracy of PET scan and CT was similar; the test is expensive and is not used for routine staging. A hybrid PET/CT system is somewhat more accurate than PET alone for detecting extra-renal lesions.
Bone scan: indicated if bony metastases are suspected (bone pain, elevated alkaline phosphatase).
MRI of brain: indicated if brain metastases are suspected.
If transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is suspected, obtain urine cytology and ureteroscopy.
Suspect renal cancer in patients with hematuria, weight loss, diaphoresis, and/or flank pain.
For patients with an incidental renal mass on CT or ultrasound, determine whether the patient is symptomatic. If symptomatic, obtain CT scan of abdomen and pelvis and order urology referral.
If asymptomatic, determine Bosniak classification of renal mass.

The Bosniak classification () is used to determine whether the renal mass is a simple cyst, benign cyst, indeterminate cystic lesion, or presumed malignant cystic mass. It is helpful in determining whether surveillance or surgical exploration and/or excision should be performed.
Consider surgery, even in the setting of metastatic disease. A

Systemic therapy with oral novel targetted agents such as sunitinib, temsirolimus, cabozantinib, or sorafenib is considered the standard of care in patients with metastatic disease. Refer to NCCN guidelines for specific recommendations. A
There is emerging evidence for benefit in first line therapy using immunotherapy agents such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab alone or combined with targetted therapy. B

A recent analysis of SEER data suggests significant increases in resection of benign renal masses with increasing risk that overtreatment with surgery may occur in small lesions This is likely due to greater use of imaging technology leading to overdiagnosis and overtreatment.
Preoperative needle biopsies are not usually obtained for resectable renal masses because of their low specificity.
Lymph node dissection is optional, but encouraged.
Radical nephrectomy is indicated if tumor extends into the inferior vena cava.

A systematic review found 18 studies comparing transperitoneal with retroperitoneal approaches for laparoscopic radical or partial nephrectomy. They concluded that a retroperitoneal approach had a shorter length of stay (by about a day), shorter operating time, and fewer complications. It is an option especially for patients with posterior tumors. However, the studies were of limited quality.

Novel ablative therapy (cryotherapy, radiofrequency ablation) may be considered in patients who are not surgical candidates. Comparative trials are limited, though. Limited evidence suggests that local control can be achieved in most patients with a low rate of adverse events. The most common schedule is 40 Gy over 5 fractions for stereotactic radiotherapy ablation.

Stage I, II, III: surgical excision. There is limited evidence to support adjuvant therapy. A double blind placebo controlled trial of 1943 patients demonstrated significant toxicity from adjuvant therapy with either sunitinib or sorafenib but no benefit on recurrence or survival. More recently, 615 patients with locregional high-risk clear cell renal cell carcinoma were randomized to sunitinib or placebo for up to 1 year. There were significantly more adverse events (60% vs 19% grade 3 or 4 adverse events), but a longer median disease-free survival (6.8 years vs 5.6 years, p = 0.03). A recent meta-analysis provides further confirmation of increased toxicity without overall survival benefit from adjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitors in high risk renal cell cancer. Radiation therapy is not indicated post nephrectomy.

A large randomised placebo controlled trial (994 patients) of pembrolizumab immunotherapy given as adjuvant treatment for a year after nephrectomy demonstrated significant benefit in disease free survival at two years (77% vs 68%, HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53-0.87). Further follow-up in this trial (KEYNOTE 564) confirms a significant overall survival benefit at 4 years (HR 0.62)..

However, benefit has not been demonstrated in a number of other adjuvant trials post-nephrectomy using immune checkpoint inhibitors including ipilimumab with nivolumab, atezolizumab single agent, or targetted drug everolimus.
For isolated, solid renal masses, resection by partial or complete nephrectomy is preferred to biopsy because it provides both the diagnosis and definitive treatment. Clinical trials are lacking.

In a single arm trial of 61 patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease, renal cell carcinoma and no evidence of metastatic disease, an objective response was seen in 49% of participants given belzutifan.
Stage IV: surgical excision (nephrectomy or cytoreductive nephrectomy and surgical metastasectomy) and/or systemic therapy.

Systemic therapy for stage IV with clear cell histology: options include sunitinib, temsirolimus (patients with poor-prognosis), bevacizumab and interferon, high-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2), pazopanib, sorafenib, and axitinib. These results are summarized in a Cochrane review. Encourage enrollment in a clinical trial. Combinations are being explored but are not standard therapy at this time. Upon disease progression, consider treatment not previously administered.

National Comprehensive Care Network guidelines for Stage IV kidney cancer with clear cell histology and a favorable prognosis recommend sunitinib, pazopanib, or axitinib plus pembrolizumab as preferred options for systemic therapy. Other recommended options include ipilimumab + nivolumab, cabozantinib, and axitinib + avelumab. For patients with a poor or intermediate risk, they preferred regimens are ipilimumab + nivolumab or axitinib + pembrolizumab. Preferred regimens for subsequent therapy include cabozantinib, nivolumab, or ipilimumab + nivolumab. For patients with non-clear cell histology, preferred regimens for systemic therapy include sunitinib or a clinical trial, with cabozantinib and everolimus as other recommended regimens.

"Targetted' agents" such as sunitinib, temsirolimus, cabozantinib, or sorafenib are protein kinase inhibitors working on a number of different biological pathways. Recent research shows benefit from more specific targetted therapy (cabozantinib: a MET kinase inhibitor) in advanced papillary renal cancer, a less common pathology.

There is emerging evidence for benefit of immunotherapy agents such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab alone or combined with targetted therapy. The newer targetted therapies may also have benefit in tolerability and quality of life as in the comparison of cabozantinib with sunitinib.
However the addition of cabozantinib to ipi/nivo combination in advanced disease suggested worse toxicity without clear benefit in a randomized trial with 855 patients.

In one RCT, everolimus prolonged survival relative to placebo in patients with metastatic RCC that had progressed on other targeted therapies. A large RCT, however, shows better progression free survival with cabozantinib than with everolimus in patients who had progressed following previous VEGFR therapy.
A large RCT (n = 821) of everolimus vs nivolumab, a PDL-1 checkpoint inhibitor, confirms significant overall survival benefit from nivolumab.

Three large RCTs have compared sunitinib as standard of care against immunotherapy agents in combination with targeted therapy in the treatment of first line metastatic disease. In those patients who are PDL1 positive, immunotherapy appears to confer benefit in progression free survival but only one study has shown a benefit in overall survival.
In patients with metastatic kidney cancer and clear cell histology, atezolizumab + bevacizumab increased progression free survival (PFS) compared with sunitinib but not overall survival.

In an RCT of 1069 patients with advanced renal cel carcinoma and no previous systemic therapy, patients were randomized to lenvatinib + pembrolizumab, lenvatinib + everolimus, or sunitinib. They found that overall survival was longer with lenvatinib + pembrolizumab than with sunitinib (HR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.49 to 0.88) but not for lenvatinib + everolimus compared with sunitinib (HR1.15; 95% CI, 0.88 to 1.50).

An RCT of 651 patients with advanced renal cell carcinoma randomized them to nivolumab + cabozantinib or sunitinib alone. Overall survival at 12 months was significantly better with combination therapy (HR 0.60, 98.89% CI 0.40-0.89). Health related quality of life was also improved more.

A study randomized 374 adults with stage IV renal cancer and a favorable Karnofsky performance score (70+) to belzutifan 120 mg or everolimus 10 mg orally once daily. At a median 26 month follow-up, overall survival was 21.4 months for belzutifan and 18 months for everolimus. Progression free survival at median 18 months was 24% for belzutifan compared with 8.3% for everolimus (p = 0.002).

Overall 5-year survival rate is 65.5%. Newer targeted therapies such as sorafenib, temsirolimus, and sunitinib have significantly improved prognosis for patients with advanced clear cell renal cancer. A
Poor prognostic indicators include elevated LDH, decreased hemoglobin, poor performance status, multiple metastatic sites, and short interval between diagnosis and initiation of systemic therapy. B
Lung metastasis is the most common site of distant recurrence.
Most disease relapse occurs within 3 years of surgery.
Overall 5-year survival for all stages is 65.5%.

The role of biomarkers in predicting disease progression and treatment response are under investigation. In particular, carbonic anhydrase IX is useful in predicting treatment response and vascular-derived growth factor has good correlation with stage and grade with increased levels predicting poorer survival.
See for prognosis by stage.

Poor prognosis is associated with three or more of the following predictors of short survival: lactate dehydrogenase greater than 1.5 times upper limit of normal, hemoglobin less than lower limit of normal, corrected calcium level greater than 10 mg/dL, interval of less than 1 year from original diagnosis to start of systemic therapy, Karnofsky performance status score of 70 or less, and two or more sites of organ metastases.

Stage I, II, III: every 6 months for 2 years (history and physical, laboratory tests including comprehensive metabolic panel and LDH); 4 to 6 months after surgery, obtain a follow-up imaging study (CT/MRI) and as clinically indicated.
Stage IV: continuous monitoring while on systemic therapy.

feature.caption: Bosniak Classification of Cystic Renal Masses.
feature.feature_body:
Class Cyst Type Radiographic Findings
I Simple benign cysts These lesions are round or oval in shape, are unilocular with the uniform density of water, have no perceptible wall, and exhibit no enhancement on radiographs taken after the administration of contrast medium.
II Probable benign simple cystic lesions that are minimally complicated These lesions include septated cysts, minimally calcified cysts, infected cysts, and high-density cysts.
III More complicated cystic lesions These lesions exhibit some findings seen in malignancy, such as thick, irregular calcifications, irregular borders, multilocular form, thickened or enhancing septa, uniform wall thickening, or small nonenhancing nodules.
IV Clearly malignant cystic masses The appearance of these lesions results from necrosis and liquefaction of a solid tumor or a tumor growing in the wall. These lesions are heterogeneous, with a shaggy appearance, thickened walls, or enhancing nodules.
Data from Bosniak MA. The current radiological approach to renal cysts. Radiology 1986;158:1-10.

feature.caption: Staging and Prognosis of Renal Cell Cancer.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Definition 5-Year Survival (%)
I Tumor <7 cm in greatest dimension and limited to kidney 95
II Tumor >7 cm in greatest dimension and limited to kidney 88
III Tumor in major veins or adrenal gland, tumor within Gerota's fascia, or one regional lymph node involved 59
IV Tumor beyond Gerota's fascia or >one regional lymph node involved 20
Data from Cohen HT, McGovern FJ. Renal-cell carcinoma. N Engl J Med 2005;353:2477-2490.
